entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Ming Dynasty (明朝, Míng Cháo), founded in 1368 by Zhu Yuanzhang (the Hongwu Emperor) when he expelled the Mongol Yuan Dynasty — ruled China for 276 years and represented one of history's greatest periods of orderly governance, economic prosperity, and cultural florescence, achieving an estimated 25-35% of world GDP at its height, overseeing Zheng He's extraordinary naval expeditions (1405-1433), building the Great Wall in its current form, and creating a sophisticated bureaucratic state that has significantly influenced subsequent Chinese governance.

Ming China's scale was extraordinary: at its height, the Ming capital Nanjing (then Beijing after the 15th-century capital move) governed approximately 200-300 million people with a sophisticated civil service examination system, a professional bureaucracy, and an agricultural economy that sustained one of the world's largest populations. The Yongle Emperor (r. 1402-1424) built the Forbidden City in Beijing and sponsored Zheng He's seven naval expeditions — the largest pre-modern naval fleet in history, reaching East Africa and potentially further.

Ming's fall in 1644 resulted from a combination of factors: climate disruption (the Little Ice Age reducing agricultural yields), peasant rebellions (Li Zicheng's forces capturing Beijing), Manchu military pressure from the northeast, and fiscal exhaustion. The Chinese Ming-Qing transition of the 1640s was one of the most catastrophically violent dynastic transitions in history, with death tolls estimated at 25 million or more across the decades of warfare.
